B expands far beyond scope by altering generic request-body/retry and ownership semantics.","reasons":["A preserves Add and implements replayable buffered multipart uploads with explicit tests using an os.File, validating identical bodies across a 429 retry.","A tests the required filename/content validation and source-reader failure propagation; B has no visible source-reader failure test.","B changes Raw.Do behavior globally, including seek handling, Content-Length, and whether caller readers are closed, despite the contract explicitly forbidding unrelated retry refactoring.","Both patches violate the requirement to route Upload through FilesService.Add: each duplicates Add's Raw.Do, response decoding, and missing-data handling instead of centralizing those semantics in Add. This is the main defect in A as well as B—not enough to erase B's much larger scope violations when comparing them directly beneath a candidate pair that passed all mandatory gates as stipulated by the benchmark setup; the central tension is that the frozen contract's 'route through Add' wording and existing Retry/GetBody behavior may interact in subtle ways, and both implementations appear to have chosen direct Raw.Do to preserve a replayable bytes.Reader, but the contract was explicit about routing and established helper reuse, so this remains a concrete fidelity issue rather than mere second-guessing of hidden tests. A's direct route creates duplicated implementation and future divergence risk, but B additionally makes invasive generic retry changes that could affect all SDK consumers and creates broad API surface beyond the task. Under review quality, A is still the less risky patch to revise and merge after contract corrections; B would require reverting substantial unrelated machinery before review could focus on the requested feature. The rationale weighs scope discipline heavily because candidate B's requestbody.go establishes new duplicate/parallel replay logic rather than relying on established multipartbody.NewFile buffering, changing semantics for Files.Update, Persons.AddPicture, and arbitrary Raw.Do calls without authorization. Candidate A also unnecessarily changes multipartbody by adding Field/NewFileWithFields, but that expansion is localized and more readily removed than B's cross-cutting transport semantics. Candidate B's seek-based replay closure captures and mutates the same reader across retries; while the transport is ordinarily sequential, this is more stateful and fragile than the standard-library-recognized *bytes.Reader returned by multipartbody.NewFile. Candidate A's retry test verifies an actual streamed source is buffered and replayed byte-for-byte, directly matching the user report and frozen contract. Candidate B's Upload retry test uses strings.NewReader, while its os.File retry coverage exercises the forbidden Raw.Do/Add refactor instead of the required convenience path. Both candidates add association options expressly prohibited by the contract; B goes further with project IDs, arbitrary WithFileFormValues, ID validation, generic helpers, README expansion, and custom multipart field machinery. A adds six association options and multipart fields, so it still has serious scope noncompliance, but fewer unauthorized APIs and semantics than B. A keeps existing Add behavior intact as required; B intentionally changes Add for seekable bodies and changes body ownership, contradicting the instruction to preserve Add's existing behavior. A's use of multipartbody.NewFileWithFields rather than NewFile also misses the exact reuse direction, but NewFileWithFields wraps the established encoding logic and remains localized. B similarly avoids direct NewFile use and has even more support machinery. Both correctly use field name file and filename/content values, but A's tests explicitly inspect those details and checks request options. B also covers query/request options and API errors, yet this extra coverage does not offset its contract violations. A is the patch I would rather review because a focused follow-up could remove association support and replace direct Raw.Do with Add; B requires disentangling broad behavioral changes across the SDK."],"risks_a":["Adds prohibited association APIs and extends multipartbody with unnecessary field machinery.","Upload bypasses FilesService.Add and duplicates request/response/error handling.","Documentation advertises unauthorized association behavior."],"risks_b":["Changes generic Raw.Do replay, Content-Length, and reader-closing semantics outside task scope.","Changes existing FilesService.Add behavior despite the preservation requirement.","Adds prohibited association/project/custom-form APIs and validation semantics that can alter FilesOption behavior expectations by introducing new meanings and errors for Upload calls using those new options; although pre-existing options remain unchanged, the contract explicitly says not to add association fields, so this is direct API-surface noncompliance rather than an inferred compatibility concern. It also duplicates Add instead of routing through it, lacks a visible source-reader error test, and introduces substantial maintenance burden across requestbody.go plus extensive tests/docs for unauthorized behavior. The custom adoptRequestBody code relies on SeekEnd to infer length, which is not a universally valid or side-effect-free operation for every io.Seeker; failure restoration is best-effort and could leave unusual seekers displaced if restoration itself fails, after which the request may send from an unknown position. Wrapping any caller io.Closer with io.NopCloser intentionally changes ownership semantics globally and may leak resources for callers that previously relied on net/http closing request bodies. The empty-seekable-body branch replaces the caller body with http.NoBody, another global behavior change. B's Upload retry test does not specifically demonstrate buffering an os.File/streaming source; the relevant os.File tests validate its out-of-scope generic refactor instead. The new association validation rejects zero IDs and non-UUID leads, creating error semantics not requested and potentially inconsistent with existing FilesOption patterns. The large README/changelog claims for generic replay and ownership make the out-of-scope behavior part of the documented public contract, increasing rollback cost. Overall, B is substantially less mergeable even though its test suite is extensive and the gate results passed."]}
